query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Alloying with oxygen-resistant elements can improve the high-temperature performance of Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr.
generation.intervention: Addition of 1-3 at.% aluminum to form a protective oxide layer
generation.conditions: Temperature: 1000 °C, Atmosphere: Air, Exposure time: Up to 100 hours
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a thin, continuous Al2O3 layer on the surface
generation.mechanism: The Al2O3 layer acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion, reducing oxidation and degradation of the underlying alloy
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved oxidation resistance without significant sacrifice of mechanical performance, with a predicted yield strength retention of 80-90% after 100 hours of exposure
generation.baseline: Untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr with 8-16% room-temperature tensile ductility and 163-530 MPa yield strength at 1000 °C
generation.boundary: Mechanical loading: Up to 500 MPa, Strain rates: 10−4–10−2 s−1
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of aluminum required for optimal performance and the potential effects on mechanical properties at lower temperatures are uncertain

falsification_experiment.design: Controlled exposure of aluminum-alloyed and unalloyed Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr samples to air at 1000 °C for up to 100 hours, followed by tensile testing at room temperature and 1000 °C
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminum-alloyed samples exhibit significantly reduced yield strength or tensile ductility compared to the unalloyed samples, or if the oxidation rate is not improved, the hypothesis is falsified
